interactions.summary: Jiang intensifies his hypothetical by having Piccarda threaten suicide rather than break her vow to God, while her brother claims his own battle vow obligates him to give her to his ally; Jiang asks the class to use imagination and intuition to decide both the likely outcome and the right choice.
A student objects that the scenario is morally warped because the brother is presuming to surrender someone else's free will and is effectively playing God.

Jiang brackets the moral objection and insists on playing out the story imaginatively; after a student suggests the brother would simply stop Piccarda from dying, Jiang replies that he cannot physically prevent an immediate suicide threat and escalates the plot to coercion through the mother.

A student asks why the brother cannot substitute another woman, and Jiang answers that the vow is binding precisely because he named Piccarda before the battle and therefore treats the scenario as fixed.

speaker_notes.note: Three separate students intervene here: one rejects the premise as a violation of free will, another tries to solve the immediate suicide problem pragmatically, and a third asks whether the brother could satisfy the vow by substituting someone else.

claims.claim: Jiang turns Piccarda's dilemma into a direct clash of vows by having her threaten suicide rather than break her vow to God while her brother insists that his victory in battle binds him to give her to his friend.
The student argues that only the person who received free will from God can surrender it back to God, so the brother's promise of Piccarda is an illegitimate seizure of her will.
claims.temporal_scope: Student counter-reading voiced in the 2026-06-16 discussion.

claims.claim: Jiang explicitly asks the class to suspend immediate moral refusal and instead use imagination and intuition to see how the conflict would actually unfold.
Jiang says the brother cannot simply save Piccarda from an immediate suicide threat, so he escalates to threatening their mother in order to force surrender.
Jiang treats the vow as person-specific: the brother cannot substitute another woman because he explicitly promised Piccarda to his ally before the battle.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang raises the stakes until vow outranks even the prohibition on suicide: Piccarda would rather die than let the church overrule her promise to God.
signature_moments.source_phrase: my vow to God is greater than the catholic church
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the extremity of Jiang's will-and-vow framework instead of softening it into a generic moral puzzle.

signature_moments.moment: The strongest pushback is that the brother is not just mistaken but acting as if he were God by surrendering another person's will.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the brother here is playing god
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's cleanest articulation of the class resistance Jiang wants the hypothetical to pressure-test.

signature_moments.moment: When Jiang decides the brother cannot stop the suicide directly, the whole thought experiment mutates into blackmail through the mother.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the turn that makes the scenario morally dense enough for Jiang's later point about intuition versus strategy.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The student's phrase for the brother presuming to dispose of Piccarda's free will as if it belonged to him.
Jiang's assumption that a vow binds the exact promised object or person, so substitution does not resolve the conflict.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-16 Jiang shifts from Piccarda's doctrinal situation to a deliberately cinematic hypothetical that escalates step by step from suicide threat to maternal blackmail in order to test what faithful choice would mean under pressure.

uncertainty_notes.note: ASR varies between Piccarda/Picardo/Ricardo and occasionally drops connective words, but the structure of Jiang's hypothetical is clear.
